#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# The estimator, the menu, its validation and the helpers of Tasks 4 to 6, as
# in R/spec_tools.R of the workspace, apart from the tag of the class chart,
# which lasts for the browser session. The data files arrive through the
# resources list of the including page, in the folder named by .data_dir.

# ============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION – the class chart and the workshop's website
# ============================================================================
# The results Form pre-filled by submit_exploration() and report_result(): its
# ID and the entry codes of its seven fields, shared by the workshop; a Form of
# its own replaces them here only. .case_word follows the tag in every label,
# and the chart of this case study reads only the rows that carry it.
.form_id <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
.form_entry <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
                 t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
                 r = "entry.1660273001")
.case_word <- "housing"
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing"
# ============================================================================


# ---- The estimator -------------------------------------------------------------
# A verbatim copy of R/_tools.R in the workshop's GitHub repository, which builds
# the curve; the downloadable workspace carries the same copy in R/spec_tools.R.

# The workspace, the browser lab and the workshop's pipeline run the
# same code. R/check_parity.R in the workshop's GitHub repository checks the HC2 errors
# and the average marginal effect against estimatr and margins.

# The options of the curve, in menu order. Anything else is refused by
# check_spec() with the reason recorded in data/menu_options.csv.
SPEC_AXES <- list(
  comparison = c("white", "nonhispanic"),
  population = c("replies", "all"),
  uncoded    = c("drop", "not_named"),
  model      = c("lpm", "logit"),
  adjust     = c("none", "email", "place", "place_ethnic")
)

# Covariates of each adjustment set; all are recorded before the emails went out.
ADJUST_TERMS <- list(
  none         = character(0),
  email        = "hard_email",
  place        = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third"),
  place_ethnic = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")
)

# The analysed rows and the outcome of one specification. Bounced emails never
# reached an official and are outside the experiment under every option.
spec_frame <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") {
  housing |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply),
                  .env$comparison == "nonhispanic" | group %in% c("white", "hispanic"),
                  .env$population == "all" | reply == 1) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
      y = dplyr::case_when(reply == 0 ~ 0,
                           is.na(named) & .env$uncoded == "not_named" ~ 0,
                           .default = named)
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(y))
}

# The conversion rules of the robustness study (standard_correlation_coefficient.R in
# github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100): t with its df, which is the rule of
# effectsize::t_to_r(); z with the sample size standing in for the missing df;
# a chi-square read as the square of a z, so it carries no sign.
r_robustness <- function(stat, stat_type, df, n) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    stat_type == "t" ~ effectsize::t_to_r(stat, df, ci = NULL)$r,
    stat_type == "z" ~ tanh(abs(stat) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3))) * sign(stat),
    stat_type == "chi2" ~ tanh(sqrt(abs(stat)) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3)))
  )
}

check_spec <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  chosen <- list(comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
                 model = model, adjust = adjust)
  bad <- names(chosen)[!purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, SPEC_AXES[names(chosen)], \(v, ok) v %in% ok)]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("Not on the curve: ", paste0(bad, " = '", unlist(chosen[bad]), "'", collapse = ", "),
         ". The options are listed in data/menu_options.csv.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# One specification: estimate in percentage points (negative = Hispanic names
# greeted by name less often, the direction of the claim), its SE and 95%
# interval, the test of the model that the specification fits, and the partial
# correlation by the rule of the robustness study.
fit_spec <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none") {
  check_spec(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
  # the data of the replication hold no hard_email, which the adjustment
  # leaves out
  terms <- intersect(ADJUST_TERMS[[adjust]], names(housing))
  # only the model columns, and only the emails with every covariate;
  # marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
  frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison, population, uncoded) |>
    dplyr::select("y", "hisp", dplyr::all_of(terms)) |>
    stats::na.omit()
  form <- stats::reformulate(c("hisp", terms), response = "y")

  if (model == "lpm") {
    fit <- stats::lm(form, data = frame)
    # HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from sandwich::vcovHC() (Zeileis
    # 2004, Journal of Statistical Software), with the t test on the residual df
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "t", stat = row$t,
                 df = row$df_error, p = row$p)
    est <- list(b = row$Coefficient, se = row$SE, low = row$CI_low, high = row$CI_high)
  } else {
    fit <- stats::glm(form, family = stats::binomial(), data = frame)
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, ci_method = "wald")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "z", stat = row$z,
                 df = NA_real_, p = row$p)
    # The average marginal effect: the mean over the analysed emails of the
    # predicted probability with a Hispanic name minus that with a comparison
    # name, with delta-method errors (marginaleffects; Arel-Bundock, Greifer and
    # Heiss 2024, Journal of Statistical Software)
    ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
    est <- list(b = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error, low = ame$conf.low, high = ame$conf.high)
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
    model = model, adjust = adjust,
    b_pp = 100 * est$b, se_pp = 100 * est$se,
    coef = test$coef, coef_se = test$coef_se,
    stat_type = test$stat_type, stat = test$stat, df = test$df, p = test$p,
    r = r_robustness(test$stat, test$stat_type, test$df, nrow(frame)),
    n = nrow(frame), n_hisp = sum(frame$hisp == 1), n_comp = sum(frame$hisp == 0),
    rate_hisp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 1]),
    rate_comp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 0]),
    ci_low = 100 * est$low, ci_high = 100 * est$high
  )
}

# The free-text label that carries a specification to the class chart.
spec_line <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  sprintf("comparison=%s population=%s uncoded=%s model=%s adjust=%s",
          comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
}


# ---- The menu --------------------------------------------------------------------
# The eleven decisions in menu order, with the options on the curve: those of
# the five decisions of SPEC_AXES multiply to the 64 specifications, and the
# other six keep one each. Every other option is a row of data/menu_options.csv,
# with its reason.
.menu <- list(
  # The question
  outcome    = "named",
  comparison = SPEC_AXES$comparison,
  population = SPEC_AXES$population,
  names      = "both",
  officials  = "any",
  # Measurement
  uncoded    = SPEC_AXES$uncoded,
  bounced    = "exclude",
  # The model
  model      = SPEC_AXES$model,
  adjust     = SPEC_AXES$adjust,
  inference  = "model",
  scale      = "pp"
)
.level_titles <- c(estimand    = "The question",
                   measurement = "Measurement",
                   estimation  = "The model")


# ---- The shipped files -----------------------------------------------------------
# Each file is read once and cached. An empty cell must read as NA: the 14
# authorities without community thirds would otherwise enter the adjusted
# models as a fourth level "".
.cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.read_once <- function(name, path) {
  if (is.null(.cache[[name]])) {
    if (!file.exists(path))
      stop(sprintf("%s not found. Reload the page.",
                   path), call. = FALSE)
    assign(name, utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8",
                                 na.strings = c("", "NA")),
           envir = .cache)
  }
  .cache[[name]]
}
.housing   <- function() .read_once("housing", file.path(.data_dir, "housing_emails.csv"))
.curve   <- function() .read_once("curve", file.path(.data_dir, "spec_curve.csv"))
.options <- function() .read_once("options", file.path(.data_dir, "menu_options.csv"))


# ---- Pages on the workshop's website ----------------------------------------------------
.pages <- c(
  "background.qmd"                = "Background",
  "menu.qmd"                      = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#map"                  = "Decision map",
  "curve.qmd"                     = "Specification curve",
  "companion/experiments.qmd"     = "Audit experiments",
  "companion/binary-outcomes.qmd" = "Binary outcomes",
  "companion/dags.qmd"            = "Causal graphs and conditioning",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"      = "The multiverse and its critics")
.page_ref <- function(path) {
  title <- if (path %in% names(.pages)) .pages[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub(".qmd", ".html", path, fixed = TRUE))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}


# ---- Validation ------------------------------------------------------------------
# .validate() checks a named list, the arguments of try_spec(); .check_choices()
# reads the eleven my_* choices of the preregistration block. An option off the
# curve stops with its reason from menu_options.csv, the page that teaches it
# and the options on the curve.
.on_menu <- function(axis, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[axis]]

.refuse <- function(axis, v, as_args) {
  shown <- if (as_args) axis else paste0("my_", axis)
  keep  <- .menu[[axis]]
  map   <- paste0("  All decisions and options: ", .page_ref("menu.qmd#map"))
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".", shown, shown, keep[1]),
         call. = FALSE)
  opts <- .options()
  row  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, .data$option == .env$v)
  off  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, !.data$on_curve)$option
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("Not on the curve of %d specifications: %s = \"%s\" (%s).",
            nrow(.curve()), shown, v, row$label),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    paste0("  Taught in: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s = %s.", shown, .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown, v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(keep, collapse = " | ")),
    if (length(off) > 0)
      sprintf("  Off the curve, refused with a reason: %s.", paste(off, collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(a) .on_menu(a, ch[[a]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], as_args)
  ch[names(.menu)]
}

# The choices are looked up from the frame of this function outwards, which
# reaches the session in which the preregistration block was run.
.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- paste0("my_", names(.menu))
  ch <- mget(need, envir = environment(), inherits = TRUE, ifnotfound = list(NULL))
  missing <- need[purrr::map_lgl(ch, is.null)]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice of the preregistration block and run the block.", call. = FALSE)
  .validate(stats::setNames(ch, names(.menu)))
}


# ---- The live fit ----------------------------------------------------------------
# fit_spec() on the five decisions that vary on the curve, with its 95%
# interval (t for the linear model, normal for the average marginal effect of
# the logit) and its place among the 64, checked against its row of
# data/spec_curve.csv.
.result <- function(ch) {
  fit <- fit_spec(.housing(), ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .curve()
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model,
                          .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1) {
    warning("This specification has no row in data/spec_curve.csv; reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  } else if (abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6 || abs(fit$stat - stored$stat) > 1e-6) {
    warning(sprintf("The fit (%.4f points, %s = %.4f) differs from data/spec_curve.csv (%.4f points, %s = %.4f). Reload the page.",
                    fit$b_pp, fit$stat_type, fit$stat, stored$b_pp, fit$stat_type, stored$stat),
            call. = FALSE)
  }
  c(fit, list(further = sum(curve$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(curve)))
}


# ---- The printout ----------------------------------------------------------------
.comparison_label <- function(comparison)
  c(white = "white names", nonhispanic = "white and Black names")[[comparison]]

.fmt_p <- function(p) sprintf("= %s", format(signif(p, 2), scientific = FALSE))

.class_line <- function(res) {
  below <- res$b_pp < 0
  sig   <- res$p < 0.05
  if (below && sig) "below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim"
  else if (below) "below zero, but not significant at 5%"
  else if (sig) "above zero and significant at 5%, against the direction of the claim"
  else "above zero and not significant at 5%"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL) {
  unit <- if (ch$population == "all") "delivered emails" else "replies"
  test <- if (res$stat_type == "t") c(
    sprintf("  Test: t = %.2f on %d df, p %s (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)",
            res$stat, round(res$df), .fmt_p(res$p))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("  Test: z = %.2f, p %s (logistic regression; the difference is its average marginal effect)",
            res$stat, .fmt_p(res$p)),
    sprintf("        logit coefficient %.3f, standard error %.3f", res$coef, res$coef_se)
  )
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", spec_line(ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust)),
    sprintf("  Greeted by name: Hispanic names %.1f%% of %d %s, %s %.1f%% of %d",
            res$rate_hisp, res$n_hisp, unit, .comparison_label(ch$comparison), res$rate_comp,
            res$n_comp),
    sprintf("  Difference: %.2f percentage points, 95%% interval %.2f to %.2f",
            res$b_pp, res$ci_low, res$ci_high),
    test,
    sprintf("  n = %d %s, partial r = %.3f (the conversion rule of the robustness study)", res$n, unit, res$r),
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %d of the %d specifications have an estimate further below zero",
            res$further, res$n_curve)))
  invisible(res)
}


# ---- Task 4: the exploratory helpers -----------------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

# The first five arguments vary on the curve; the other six are fixed on it,
# and any other option of theirs is refused with its reason.
try_spec <- function(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none", outcome = "named", names = "both",
                     officials = "any", bounced = "exclude", inference = "model", scale = "pp") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, comparison = comparison, population = population,
                       names = names, officials = officials, uncoded = uncoded,
                       bounced = bounced, model = model, adjust = adjust,
                       inference = inference, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b_pp = res$b_pp, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,
                    stat_type = res$stat_type, stat = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", dplyr::bind_rows(.tried$log, row), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The log of every fit of try_spec(), with only the decisions that varied.
my_experiments <- function() {
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet. Run try_spec() first.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  varied <- purrr::keep(names(.menu), \(a) dplyr::n_distinct(d[[a]]) > 1)
  show <- d |>
    dplyr::transmute(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(varied)),
                     estimate = round(.data$b_pp, 2),
                     interval = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", .data$ci_low, .data$ci_high),
                     test = sprintf("%s = %.2f", .data$stat_type, .data$stat),
                     p = signif(.data$p, 2),
                     n = .data$n)
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications tried: %d (estimates in percentage points)\n", nrow(d)))
  # wide enough for all five varied decisions on one line
  old_width <- options(width = max(getOption("width"), 120))
  on.exit(options(old_width))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nEstimates from %.2f to %.2f points  |  below zero and significant at 5%%: %d of %d",
                     min(d$b_pp), max(d$b_pp), sum(d$b_pp < 0 & d$p < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

submit_exploration <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  if (is.null(.tried$last))
    stop("Nothing to submit. Run try_spec() first; the last specification tried is submitted.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .submit(.tried$last$ch, .tried$last$res, "explore",
          "Exploratory submission (the last specification tried):", nickname)
}


# ---- Task 5: the declared helpers --------------------------------------------------
# prereg() prints the block and returns it, so that run_spec() can check that
# the block has not changed since.
prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  rows <- .options() |>
    dplyr::filter(paste(.data$axis, .data$option) %in% paste(names(ch), unlist(ch))) |>
    dplyr::arrange(match(.data$axis, names(.menu))) |>

# replicate_spec() fits the declared specification on the data of the

# without a greeting code, no hard_email) with each change printed, checks the
# fit against data/replication_curve.csv and places it among the 12
# specifications to which the 64 collapse on the new data.
replicate_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "housing_prereg"))
    stop("Pass the object that prereg() returned: my_spec <- prereg(), then replicate_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  ch <- spec$choices
  new <- utils::modifyList(ch, list(comparison = "white", uncoded = "drop",
                                    adjust = if (ch$adjust == "email") "none" else ch$adjust))
  changes <- c(
    if (ch$comparison == "nonhispanic")
      "  comparison = \"white\": the new experiment used no Black names.",
    if (ch$uncoded == "not_named")
      "  uncoded = \"drop\": every reply of the new experiment carries a greeting code.",
    if (ch$adjust != "none")
      "  adjust: without hard_email, which the new data do not hold.")
  fit <- fit_spec(.read_once("replication", file.path(.data_dir, "housing_replication.csv")),
                  new$comparison, new$population, new$uncoded, new$model, new$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .read_once("replication_curve", file.path(.data_dir, "replication_curve.csv"))
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model, .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1 || abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6)
    warning("The fit on the new data differs from data/replication_curve.csv. Reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  distinct <- dplyr::filter(curve, !duplicated(.data$rep_spec))
  .print_result(ch, .result(ch), "Declared specification on the original data:")
  writeLines(c("", "Declared specification on the data of the replication:",
               if (length(changes) > 0) changes
               else "  No translation: every choice exists in the new data."))
  .print_result(new, c(fit, list(further = sum(distinct$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(distinct))))
}

## SCORE in brief {#score-in-brief .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Repetition | The study | What came back |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| **Reproduction** – same data, same analysis | The SCORE reproducibility study: 600 papers from 62 journals, 2009–2018 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial] | Of the 143 that could be assessed, **53.6%** reproduced precisely and **73.5%** at least approximately; counting the papers that nobody could check, about **18%** |
| **Robustness** – same data, other analyses | The SCORE robustness study: 100 studies, at least 5 analysts each [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] | **74%** of reanalyses reached the same conclusion; **34%** came within ±0.05 *d* of the original effect size |
| **Replication** – new data | The SCORE replicability study: 274 claims, independent data [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] | **55.1%** significant again; the median effect size fell from *r* = 0.25 to 0.10 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Measured on the same body of papers, the three are **essentially uncorrelated**: knowing how a finding fared on one tells you almost nothing about the others.
:::

::: notes
SCORE, a programme funded by the research agency of the US Department of Defense, took a sample of social-science papers and put their central claims through each of the three repetitions on the grid. Reproduction first: of six hundred papers, the authors supplied data for about a quarter, and of the hundred and forty-three that could be assessed, about half reproduced precisely and three quarters approximately. Count the papers that nobody could check, and the rate is about eighteen per cent. Robustness was the subject of the SCORE robustness study, where at least five analysts reanalysed each claim: three quarters reached the same conclusion, but only a third came close to the original effect size. Replication on new data: fifty-five per cent significant again, with effect sizes more than halved. [advance] And the three barely predict one another, so for any one paper you have to ask which of the three it passed.
:::

## What an analyst of the robustness study received {#what-an-analyst-received .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, usually taken from the abstract
- The **data**, or directions for fetching them
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; preregistration of the robustness study, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–5.
:::

::: notes
The SCORE robustness study handed a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, on a different paper from the one we work on today. Let me describe what that was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was the published paper, the whole thing and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, usually taken from the abstract, and the data or directions for fetching them. What did not arrive was any instruction on method: analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what any of them were finding. The isolation was part of the design, because it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## The two tasks of the robustness study {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion out of four, evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived. It asked for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, and it came with a short instruction for each claim that pinned down one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that question can only be asked once everyone is answering roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We will read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. The robustness study converted those onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on the same axis. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread that comes out of the study is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and a good deal of what follows is about what happens when they do not. The other is that each conversion counts the units that actually carry the evidence.
:::

## The question of the paper {#the-question-of-the-paper .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The question.** Do the officials who control access to a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Officials who deal with the public directly, and decide how much help to give, are **street-level bureaucrats** [@Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy]
- **The method.** An **audit study** sends matched requests, or matched applicants, that differ in one characteristic, and compares what comes back [@BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg; @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord]. Here the characteristic is a name
- **What it added.** Audits of politicians and local election officials had found discrimination [@ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate; @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote]. This one asks about a bureaucracy that hands out a valuable benefit and is less tied to politics
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The paper is an experiment published in 2017 [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. From here on I call its two authors **the original authors (OAs)**.
:::

::: notes
The case study that we work on today is a paper in the American Journal of Political Science, and I will call its two authors the original authors, or OAs, from here on, because the workshop is about the claim and its analyses rather than about the people who made it. The question is old and important: do the officials who stand between citizens and a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Sociologists call those officials street-level bureaucrats, after Lipsky, because they deal with the public directly and have discretion over how much help to give. The method is the audit study, which sends matched requests that differ in one characteristic and compares the responses. Earlier audits had found discrimination by politicians and election officials. The OAs asked whether the same holds in a bureaucracy that hands out something valuable, access to public housing, and is further from politics.

- The reply is a **consequence of the name**, and a common effect of the name and the official: a **collider**

::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is **post-treatment conditioning**: the gap among replies mixes an effect on **how** officials write with a difference in **which** officials wrote [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment; @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias].
:::

::: notes
Now draw a box around the reply, because that is what the paper does when it compares greetings among replies only. The reply is caused by the name, and also by the official, so it is a common effect of the two, a collider. Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its causes: among the replies, the name and the official are no longer independent. If a Hispanic name discourages some officials from replying, the officials who answered Santiago are a different mix from those who answered Brett, perhaps the more conscientious ones, perhaps the busier ones. Their habits of greeting then travel along the red path into the comparison. [advance] The general name for this is post-treatment conditioning, conditioning on something that the treatment can change, and it can produce a gap even where the name has no effect on tone at all. Coppock wrote about it for exactly this kind of audit experiment.
:::

## Counting every delivered email {#counting-every-delivered-email .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Count **every delivered email**, with no reply counted as no greeting: no box, nothing opened, and the groups stay as randomisation made them
- The outcome changes with it: a **reply that greets the sender by name**, which combines whether a reply came with how it began
:::

::: {.small}
| Emails counted | Hispanic names | White names | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coded replies (n = 362) | 41.2% | 61.1% | −19.97 points |
| Delivered emails (n = 662) | 21.6% | 35.0% | −13.34 points |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two defensible questions. Among the replies: the question of the claim, about tone, but an effect of the name alone only if the name did not change who replied. Among all emails: an effect of the name that randomisation protects, on a different outcome. The reply gap of −4.8 points (p = 0.214) makes a large selection unlikely, without ruling it out.
:::

::: notes
The remedy is to remove the box. Count every email that arrived, and treat an email that drew no reply as one that drew no greeting. Now nothing is conditioned on, and the groups are exactly as the random number generator made them. But the outcome has changed with the denominator: it is now a reply that greets the sender by name, which combines whether a reply came with how it began. Among replies, forty-one per cent against sixty-one, a gap of twenty points. Among all delivered emails, twenty-two against thirty-five, a gap of thirteen. [advance] Neither is wrong. The comparison among replies answers the question of the claim, about tone, and is clean only if the name did not change who replied. The comparison among all emails is clean by design, and answers a related but different question. One of the five analysts made exactly this move.
:::

::: {.small}
- Among the replies with a greeting code, **41.2%** of the 187 replies to Hispanic names opened with the name of the sender, against **61.1%** of the 175 replies to white names
- The difference: **−19.97 percentage points**
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A linear model of a 0/1 outcome on a 0/1 indicator of the group gives exactly that difference as its coefficient. This is the **linear probability model**, and its coefficient reads directly in the units of the claim.

```{.r}

```
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Its test, with HC2 standard errors: *t* = −3.87 on 360 df, p = 0.0001.

::: notes
The statistics of this case study are about as simple as statistics gets, which is why it is a good case study to learn on. Among the coded replies, forty-one per cent of those to Hispanic names opened with the name of the sender, against sixty-one per cent of those to white names. The difference is twenty percentage points, and that difference is the estimate. [advance] You can get the same number from a regression. Fit a linear model of the greeting, coded zero or one, on an indicator that is one for the Hispanic names, and its coefficient is exactly the difference between the two shares. That model is called the linear probability model, and its great virtue is that its coefficient is already in the units of the claim. [advance] Its test, with the standard errors that the workshop uses throughout, gives a t of minus three point eight seven.

## Linear probability model and logit {#linear-probability-model-and-logit .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Linear probability model**

- The coefficient is the difference in proportions
- Simple, and in the units of the claim
- With covariates it can predict shares below 0 or above 1
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Logistic regression (logit)**

- Models the log odds of a greeting; the coefficient of the Hispanic names is −0.810, with *z* = −3.771 (UYV3F)
- Its **average marginal effect**, the change in the predicted share averaged over the emails, is on the workshop's scale
- Predicted shares always stay between 0 and 1
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Without covariates a logit reproduces the two observed shares exactly, so its average marginal effect is the same −19.97 points. Across the curve, the logit moves the estimate by −0.01 points on average against its linear twin.
:::

::: notes
The paper itself used a different model, the logistic regression or logit, which models the log odds of a greeting rather than its share. Its coefficient, minus point eight one here, is on the scale of log odds, and the z that goes with it is exactly the value recorded in the robustness study for UYV3F. To put a logit on the scale of the claim, you take its average marginal effect: predict the share of greetings for every email as if it carried a Hispanic name and as if it carried a white one, and average the difference. [advance] With no covariates the logit reproduces the two observed shares exactly, so its average marginal effect is the same twenty points. With covariates the two models part a little, and across the whole curve the choice between them moves the estimate by a hundredth of a point on average. The model is a decision on the menu that barely matters here.
:::

## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Multiverse background, 2 slides – skip to the curve →](#the-curve-of-the-claim)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – developed for *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Under all these names the proposal is the same: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
A brief history, because the vocabulary is a mess and knowing which word came from where helps. Multiverse analysis is Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of data-processing choices specifically – how you code a variable, which cases you exclude, how you combine items – with the proposal that you report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis is Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, making the same move for model choices and adding a visual grammar: estimates plotted on top, and underneath them a panel showing which choices produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea arrived at independently in epidemiology, which suggests that it is a natural response to the problem. And there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. Under different names, they all make the same proposal: stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.
:::

Its names were different, all male, and pre-tested to vary ethnicity without varying class. It coded a friendly reply as any use of a name, which is close to the lenient coding of the original but not identical. Its census covariates come from a later year. And it is later in time. ## Power of the two designs {#power-of-the-two-designs}


::: {.cell}

The original comparison detects a gap of 20 points almost always (0.97), but one of 10 points less than half the time (0.48). The replication has 0.78 for 10 points.
:::

::: notes
One more lens: power, the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. At a white share of sixty-one per cent, the original comparison, with about a hundred and eighty replies a group, detects a twenty-point gap almost every time. But its power for a ten-point gap is under one half, and for thirteen points about seven in ten. The replication, with three hundred and sixty-nine replies a group, has nearly eight in ten for ten points. Two consequences. A replication of this size would have found a gap of ten points about four times in five, and a larger one more often still, had there been one. And when a study with modest power for realistic effects does reach significance, its estimate tends to overstate the true effect, because only the lucky draws clear the bar. The published interval runs from minus thirty to minus ten.
:::

Robustness, on the original data, holds in the strongest sense that a curve can offer: every analysis that the workshop judged justifiable, and every one of the five analysts, finds the gap in the same direction and significant, and only its size moves. By the rule of the robustness study, though, which counts a claim as robust only when every reanalyst finds evidence for it, this claim would not count, because two of the five did not. Replication with new data found nothing. So the one paper has a different answer for each R, and they do not line up.
:::

## Robustness and replicability {#robustness-and-replicability}

:::: {.none .fs-85}
::: {.fragment}
On the original data, every justifiable analysis finds the gap. Only its size moves.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every one of those analyses uses the same 1,014 emails, the same six names, the same officials in the same year. **The curve varies the analysis and never the sample.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
So robustness to analytic choices on one sample is not replicability.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Candidates for the difference: the **names** [@Gaddis2017HowBlackAre], **chance**, and **time and place**.
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the case study's lesson, and the workshop's. On the original data the claim is hard to dislodge: every justifiable analysis finds the gap, and only its size moves. [advance] But every one of those analyses works on the same thousand emails, the same six names, the same officials in the same week of 2014. A specification curve varies the analysis and holds the sample fixed, so it cannot tell you what a new sample would show. [advance] Robustness to analytic choices on one sample is a different property from replicability. [advance] Why might the two studies differ? The names are one candidate: names that are meant to indicate one group are not all read the same way, and Santiago and Gabriela may also have read as younger. Chance is another, given the power of the original design. And time and place are a third. The replication does not tell us which.
:::

## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
The first point comes from the paper on the robustness study: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. A single path can be a good path, and still the reader is owed the space around it, so a report needs the chosen path and the alternatives together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive recipe that we followed today: a precise question, explicit assumptions drawn as a graph, a multiverse, and a sensitivity analysis. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: the same conclusion, which was reached by seventy-four per cent of the reanalyses in the robustness study, and the same number, which only thirty-four per cent came close to. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::
